title: Count the stars (Genesis 15:1–6)
hook: a childless old man is told to count the stars, and believes

segments.voice: Yesterday, bread and wine, Melchisedech: a priest-king on the road, and a blessing. Your line was bread and wine, long ago. Which bite did you take slowly? Day three hundred forty-seven.

Abram has land promised, a great name promised, a nation promised. What he doesn't have is a single child. Years have gone by since he left home. He's won a war and been blessed by a king, and still the tent is quiet. So when God speaks to him in a vision and says fear not, I am thy reward, Abram finally says the hard thing out loud. What will you give me? I'm going childless, and a servant in my house, Eliezer of Damascus, is going to inherit everything. It's the first time in the story Abram argues back. And God's answer is to take him outside.
screen: `EVERYTHING PROMISED BUT A CHILD.` → `WHAT WILL YOU GIVE ME?` → `GOD TAKES HIM OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the sky. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he brought him forth abroad, and said to him: Look up to heaven and number the stars, if thou canst. And he said to him: So shall thy seed be." Picture it with no city lights at all. Thousands of stars, the river of the Milky Way. God doesn't answer the complaint with an argument. God gives Abram something to look at. Count them, if you can. Second, the response, one short verse: "Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice." Reputed means counted, credited. Unto justice means as righteousness. The Hebrew verb for believed comes from the same root as amen: to be firm, to lean your weight on something. Abram leans his weight on the promise. Nothing has changed yet. He's still old, Sarai's still childless, the tent's still quiet. He believes anyway. Third, the line's long life. Saint Paul quotes it in his letters to the Romans and the Galatians: Abraham believed, and it was counted to him. The Letter of James quotes it too, and sets it beside Abraham's deeds. Catholics read Paul and James together: a faith that is alive, and shows itself in love. Many Protestant churches put the emphasis on faith alone. In 1999, Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of this, while still differing on some points. Fourth, the stars themselves. The Letter to the Hebrews looks back on this night: from one man, and him as good as dead, came children as many as the stars of heaven. Paul calls Abraham the father of all who believe, which is why Catholics speak of him as our father in faith. Jews and Muslims call him father too. A man who couldn't see one grandchild was asked to look up anyway.
screen: `NUMBER THE STARS, IF THOU CANST.` · `ABRAM BELIEVED GOD.` · `THE SAME ROOT AS AMEN.` · `PAUL AND JAMES BOTH QUOTE IT.` · then, large: `SO SHALL THY SEED BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the night sky. If it's night where you are, step outside or go to a window. If it's daytime, close your eyes and remember the clearest night sky you've ever seen. Settle, and breathe. Start counting, slowly. One. Two. Three. Don't rush. Somewhere past ten you'll lose your place. Let yourself lose it. Notice how big the sky is and how small the counting is. If you pray, you can name a promise you're still waiting on, and leave it up there. The bell holds the time.
Amen, the root behind Abram believed: to be firm, to lean your weight on a promise before anything has changed. Today's word.
Your line: so shall thy seed be. Tonight, look up for one minute before bed, even through a window, and remember someone who's still waiting on something. Day three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics call Abraham their father in faith, and Genesis 15:5–6 is read with Paul's letters in the liturgy; the Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith.

original.note: Hebrew: he believed, he trusted. from the root of amen, to be firm.

trapdoor: what you thought: Abram is promised a lot of grandchildren.
what it means: an old man with nothing to show yet leans his whole weight on a promise, and that trust is counted as righteousness.
what a scholar hears: he'emin, from the root of amen; Genesis 15:6 is quoted by Paul and by James, and churches read them in different balances.

Faith and works: Catholic reading of Paul and James together (faith working through love, Galatians 5:6), many Protestants emphasizing faith alone; 1999 Joint Declaration with the Lutheran World Federation (a 'differentiated consensus'). Described without ranking; confirm.
Jews and Muslims also call Abraham father: stated briefly as neighbors who share; confirm tone.
Eliezer of Damascus (15:2): the Douay-Rheims wording is 'the son of the steward of my house is this Damascus Eliezer'; paraphrased.
